name: Agentic Drafting and Multi-Model Workflows
title: Agentic Drafting and Multi-Model Workflows
answer: Agentic drafting and multi-model workflows cover the use of AI systems that can plan, draft, revise, and route narrative tasks across more than one language model. In literary arts and narrative design, this includes generating prose, dialogue, scene outlines, and style variants, then having a separate model critique or edit the output. The scope also covers orchestration where a coordinator agent decides which model handles a given passage based on tone, length, or genre. These workflows are distinct from single-prompt generation because the system makes intermediate decisions without a human at every step.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These workflows run on hosted model APIs or locally served open-weight models, connected through an orchestration layer such as a Python script, a node-based tool, or a commercial agent platform. A typical setup keeps a project bible, character sheets, and prior chapters in a vector database or plain text store that the agent can query for continuity. Context window limits and token costs shape how much material is passed to each model at each step. Some teams run a fast small model for drafting and a slower large model for final polish or consistency checking.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is usually done by breaking a narrative task into discrete steps: outline, draft, critique, revise, and fact-check or lore-check. An agent may be given a goal and a set of tools, such as search over the project bible or a style guide, and allowed to loop until a stopping condition is met. Multi-model routing assigns each step to a model chosen for that strength, for example one model for natural dialogue and another for dense descriptive prose. Human writers typically review the agent's plan and final text, and may edit the intermediate prompts or reject a step to steer the next iteration.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in agentic drafting turn on who authored the final work, what the model provider's terms say about ownership of outputs, and whether training data included copyrighted texts. Provenance is harder to trace when several models contribute and an agent rewrites passages, so studios and publishers often keep logs of prompts, model versions, and intermediate drafts. Risk includes inadvertent plagiarism, inconsistent voice, and disclosure obligations in contracts or submission guidelines. Some jurisdictions treat purely machine-generated text as lacking copyright protection, while human selection and arrangement of agent output may qualify, but this is an evolving area of practice rather than settled law.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Agentic drafting is moving toward longer-horizon tasks where a system maintains a consistent story world across a novel, game script, or serialized fiction with less human re-prompting. Multi-model workflows are likely to become more standardized, with shared evaluation benchmarks for narrative quality and continuity. The next practical step is better memory and tool use, so an agent can revise chapter twelve against a change made in chapter three without losing voice. Human writers will likely shift further into directing, editing, and setting constraints rather than producing every sentence.
